title: Cancer Control and Population Sciences Research Program
text: CANCER CONTROL AND POPULATION SCIENCES (CCPS): ABSTRACT The goal of the CCPS program is to reduce cancer incidence and mortality in rural North Central Florida and beyond. The CCPS program’s specific aims are to: 1) Elucidate molecular, behavioral, environmental, and other risk factors in cancer incidence and mortality; 2) Develop and evaluate primary and secondary cancer prevention interventions; and 3) Address the unique needs of cancer survivors. Research activities are unified by CCPS priorities that address cancer outcomes in the catchment area (CA): a) supportive care needs; b) smoking and other tobacco use; c) molecular and imaging markers; d) obesity, energy balance, and cancer; and e) the intersection of cancer and aging. To capture the research strengths at the University of Florida (UF), CCPS assembled 48 members drawing a wide range of expertise from 20 departments and 10 colleges. The organization of CCPS has a culture of multidisciplinary collaboration with other UFHCC programs, shared resources, Community Outreach and Engagement (COE), and Cancer Research Training and Education, enabling research excellence across the translational spectrum. Since 2016, key achievements of the program include evaluating the performance of breast cancer screening in older individuals, developing novel cancer communication strategies to increase colorectal cancer screening and strengthen cancer risk reduction efforts, performing studies that informed raising the age of tobacco sale in Florida, developing radiation dosing tools to prevent harmful effects of diagnostic and therapeutic radiation, assessing Hepatitis C treatments that reduce liver cancer risk, and developing digital patient-reported outcome tools. Since 2016, program members published 1,114 cancerrelevant publications, ~7% with impact factors >10. CCPS members enrolled 6,528 participants on interventional trials, including a pragmatic clinical trial examining patientreported outcomes following proton therapy among older men with prostate cancer, and 13,064 participants on non- interventional studies. Through our efforts, robust collaboration is evident with 40% intra-programmatic, 29% inter-programmatic, and 73% multi-institutional publications. CCPS members hold >$11.5M in external peer- reviewed funding (up 48% since 2019), with >$3.7M from the NCI. CCPS mentors trained 186 graduate students and 30 postdocs. CCPS future directions are aligned with the UFHCC strategic plan, Momentum 2027, seeking further recruitments, scientific progress, and impact building on the research expertise of the UFHCC and community partnerships. Driven by the CA needs, future development includes expansion of tobacco control research, cancer communication, and screening. CCPS will address the intersectional problems of aging and cancer, obesity and cancer, and the impact of supportive care interventions on cancer outcomes. In partnership with COE, CCPS will disseminate research findings and best practices across the CA and beyond.

title: Diversity and function of TRIO isoforms during human synapse development
text:
TRIO is a high-confidence risk gene for neurodevelopmental disorders and a critical regulator of synaptic
function. However, the impact of TRIO and its isoforms on human synapse development is poorly understood.
Here we will employ cutting-edge long-read sequencing and human iPSC models to fully characterize the
diversity, expression, and function of TRIO isoforms in the human brain, revealing essential biology underlying
human synapse development and neurodevelopmental disorders.

title: Correction of Neurological Disease via Allele Specific Excision of Pathogenic Repeats
text:
Neurodegenerative diseases resulting from nucleotide triplet expansions, such as HD and ALS, lack any
disease-modifiying therapy. We will establish a first-in-class paradigm for the use of in vivo gene editing for
these diseases - allele-specific excision of the disease-causing expansion - and reduce it to preclinical and
regulatory practice. To this end we will (i) develop a mutually synergistic suite of CRISPR-Cas9 preclinical
leads for both mutant HTT and mutant C9ORF92; (ii) using multiple innovative viral and nonviral delivery
formulations, perform IND-enabling preclinical pharmacology, toxicology, CMC, and biodistribution studies; (iii)
advance an AAV-formulated CRISPR-Cas approach for HD to IND, and for ALS - to pre-IND.

title: Targeting androgen-driven resistance to immune checkpoint inhibitors in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma
text:
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) exhibits significant sex-based disparities in immune
responses, limiting the efficacy of current immunotherapies. Our research identifies Vasoactive Intestinal Peptide
receptor 1 (VPAC1) as a novel macrophage immune checkpoint that suppresses anti-tumor immunity, with
distinct regulatory mechanisms in males and females. By targeting VPAC1 in females and combining VPAC1
blockade with androgen receptor inhibition in males, we aim to develop a precision immunotherapy strategy that
enhances macrophage phagocytosis, reinvigorates adaptive immunity, and improves PDAC treatment
outcomes.

title: Development of novel therapeutics targeting the identified pathways associated with human longevity
text:
The overall goal of this U19 is to use genetic variation in human populations linked to extreme phenotypes of
healthy aging, centenarians and super-centenarians, to identify rare variants in genes and pathways important
for human aging for guiding drug development. Project 4 will focus on developing therapeutics targeting these
identified rare variants and pathways, leading to new drugs for extending healthy lifespan.

title: Defining Genome Stability Mechanisms and their Regulation by SUMO and Ubiquitin
text:
To develop effective preventative and therapeutic strategies it is vital that we define the cellular pathways and
mechanisms that suppress diseases such as cancer. In this proposal we would determine how two small, but
potent proteins called SUMO and ubiquitin orchestrate the genome stability and viral/plasmid repression
machinery. Vitally, apart from the much-needed fundamental knowledge we would gain, the SUMO and
ubiquitin pathways offer therapeutic possibilities that our analyses would help exploit.

title: 12th Aquatic Models of Human Diseases conference
text:
Aquatic animals are essential experimental platforms for biomedical research and provide powerful systems to
model human disease. The 12th Aquatic Models for Human Disease conference will bring together established
investigators, early-stage investigators, postdoctoral researchers, and graduate students from across the
United States to share advances in the use of aquatic models to study human disease. Through the theme
Emerging Models in Human Health, this conference will promote the continued development, innovation, and
integration of aquatic model systems within NIH-funded biomedical research.

title: Pharmacological targeting of nascent modulators of opioid signaling
text:
Drug addiction is a disorder of the brain that puts a heavy burden on the society. Studies proposed herein are
aimed at developing means for brain circuit selective manipuations with opioid receptor signaling aimed at
dissociating analgesic effects of opioid drugs from the development of dependence. It is anticipated that the
results will facilitate the design of novel strategies for the treatment of drug addiction addressing a critical need
to combat growing opioid abuse epidemic.

title: Mitochondrial biogenesis and transfer to promote muscle regeneration
text:
Muscle degeneration, characterized by progressive deposition of extracellular matrix (ECM) proteins
and adipocytes (fibro-fatty degeneration) is a central finding in many musculoskeletal disease
processes and is associated with a shortened lifespan. Fibroadipoprogenitor cells (FAPs) have been
found to be the central regulator of fibro-fatty degeneration, but we have shown that given the proper
stimulus (B-agonist pharmacologic treatment, blood flow restriction), they are able to differentiate into
a pro-myogenic beige fat state that stimulates muscle regeneration. In this study, we will evaluate the
mechanisms of beige-FAP mediated muscle regeneration, focusing on mitochondrial transfer as a
novel means by which FAPs can stimulate muscle regeneration and improve outcomes in several
musculoskeletal conditions that affect the aging VA population.

title: MOLECULAR MECHANISMS UNDERLYING INTELLECTUAL DISABILITY CAUSED BY MUTATIONS IN THE CHROMATIN MODIFIER KDM5C
text:
Intellectual developmental disabilities (IDD) are frequently diagnosed during early childhood and have dramatic 
quality of life consequences for the affected individual and their caregiver(s). Significant insight into brain 
mechanisms of IDDs can be gained by studying single gene mutation IDD conditions such as the one we focus 
on here, KDM5C, with the use of animal models and human cerebral organoids. In addition to providing critical 
information regarding the etiology of this cause of IDD, our work has broad implications for other known 
genetic causes of IDD.

title: Pyroptosis is a Trial-by-Fire Program
text:
Evolution tends to improve or remove a gene that is bad at what it does. A gene that nominally causes cell death
often fails to kill cells; yet it is still found across many organisms and actively utilized. Perhaps we mis-understood
its true, underlying functions? We refocus its role as a “trial-by-fire” and outline the novel tools and methods we
will use to examine the evolutionary benefits that allowed this gene family to thrive and diversify.

title: Incretin Mimetics for Intercepting Obesity-Related Cancers: Effects and Underlying Mechanisms
text:
Obesity increases the risk that cancer will develop and progress, and ways to decrease that risk are needed.
The proposed project will establish, in mice and humans with obesity, whether and how different incretin
mimetics (weight loss medications) affect development and progression of two prevalent obesity-related
cancers (endometrial, and colorectal). Project results will steer future research and provide practical guidance
on incretin mimetic use as a cancer interception strategy for individuals with obesity.

title: Research training in respiratory biology
text:
Diseases of the respiratory system and of critical illness constitute major public health problem in the US and
worldwide. The objective of this Program is to prepare young scientists to pursue research careers addressing
mechanisms and treatment of human disease, with a focus on respiratory disease and critical illness. We
expect that trainees from this Program will identify disease mechanisms and develop and implement new
effective treatments that will improve human health.

title: Tissue-resident NK cell development and function in pregnancy and transplantation: lessons learned from human uterus transplant recipients
text:
Pregnancy complications are common in organ transplant recipients, but little is understood
about the mechanisms of pathogenesis. Uterine natural killer cells have important roles in
pregnancy well-being and are altered by immunosuppression medications taken by transplant
recipients. We use a unique model of human uterus transplantation to better understand how
immunosuppression agents impact the normal function of uterine natural killer cells and lead to
complex pregnancy.

title: Exploiting Public Metagenomic Data to Uncover Cancer-Microbiome Relationships
text:
The human microbiome is implicated in the development and response to treatment of some cancers, including
infectious agents estimated to be responsible for ~20% of the global cancer burden. However, previously
unrecognized bacterial and viral strains, as well as loss of normal structure and function of human-associated
microbiomes, likely play additional roles in disease etiology and treatment. This project investigates the role of
the human microbiome in cancer by applying novel and state-of-the-art methods to published metagenomic
data, and provides enhanced, expanded, and more efficiently usable microbiome data resources back to the
cancer research community for a broad range of investigations.

title: Uncovering DIP-α signaling pathways underlying circuit assembly
text:
Establishing specific synaptic connections is critical for proper neural circuit function, and alterations in
connectivity have been linked to neurological diseases such as Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s diseases. This
proposal will investigate how two subfamilies of cell surface proteins, the Dprs and DIPs, instruct specific
connectivity in Drosophila central motor circuits. This study will also examine the signaling mechanisms
underlying Dpr and DIP interactions, and potentially provide new signaling insights into their vertebrate
orthologs, the IgLONs, which are associated with various neurological diseases.

title: Biomechanical and biomolecular characterization of large extracellular vesicles
text:
Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are cell fragments found throughout the body that carry various biomolecules
(proteins, nucleic acids, lipids) and are potential circulating biomarkers for diagnosing various diseases from
simple blood samples and potential drug delivery vehicles for delivering drugs to hard-to-reach places. Before
EVs can be leveraged in these ways, more research on their basic properties and better tools to perform these
characterizations are needed. The overall goal of this project is to investigate new EV subtypes and their
clinical potential using our microfluidic technology that will be advanced to measure the biomechanical and
biomolecular properties of single L-EVs simultaneously.

title: Finding effective T-cell receptors for infectious diseases based on receptor sequences
text:
There are billions of unique T cells surveying our bodies to protect us from invading organisms, such as
bacteria and viruses, and various diseases. In this project, we propose to create a platform to facilitate finding
T-cell receptors (TCRs) that can recognize the pathogen and activate our immune system for defense. The
platform and computational methods that we develop will be valuable in discovering crucial pathogen-targeting
TCRs, which can be leveraged for disease diagnosis, monitoring, and treatment.

title: Bioinformatics, Statistical and Methodological Shared Resources Core
text: The primary goal of the Bioinformatics, Statistical, and Methodological Core (BSMC) at the Florida-California Cancer Research, Education & Engagement (CaRE2) Health Center is to provide the data management, data cleaning, data storage, and data release to public databases for all information generated by our Center. In addition, it will provide bioinformatics, statistical and methodological support for all the cancer research projects proposed, as well as future projects that will build upon them and will be disseminated to all CaRE2 Center members and the scientific community at large in a timely fashion. We will reach these goals through three aims: First, we will provide bioinformatics, statistical, and methodological support. This first aim is to establish the job scheduling and interfaces to meet the needs of all CaRE2 Health Center investigators. We will support bioinformatics and statistical issues across the projects and cores. Bioinformatics support will include in-depth quality control and assessment of all high-throughput sequencing data from multiple platforms and facilitate access to publicly available datasets. Statistical and methodological support will consist of all data management, from collecting data to state-of-the-art data analysis and interpretation as well as abstract, manuscript, and grant preparation. The second aim will be enhancing and maintaining a federated data repository resource that enables the interaction of CaRE2 members. This second aim will ensure that all data are of high quality and disseminated promptly to all CaRE2 Center members and the scientific community. In the third aim, we will provide bioinformatics, statistical, and methodological educational opportunities to the CaRE2 Center. This third aim focuses on developing online educational materials that BSMC's members and guest experts will present through the core events, such as seminar series and interactive lectures among all CaRE2 Center members.

title: VIBRATOME
text:
The requested vibratome will produce high quality tissue sections enabling researchers at
resource-limited East Tennessee State University to study disease at the cellular level with
greater accuracy and reproducibility. Its use will advance our institution’s capacity to produce
high-impact biomedical research for the advancement of critical health issues including
neurological disorders and heart disease while providing invaluable hands-on training to the
next-generation of scientists.
